claims.text: An integrated framework coupling machine-learning-enhanced molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and refined CALPHAD can predict melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Density functional theory calculations can be used to train the machine-learning model that enhances the molecular-dynamics simulations.
Coupling molecular-simulation outputs to a CALPHAD thermodynamic model enables prediction of phase transitions and liquid-phase properties.
Atomic-level configurational disorder and the resulting potential-energy landscape mediate phase transitions in high-entropy alloys.
The configurationally disordered energy landscape determines liquid structure and changes in enthalpy, entropy, and volume during melting.
High configurational entropy is intrinsic to high-entropy alloys.
The machine-learning component can capture complex multielement interaction energies and vibrational contributions.
CALPHAD can systematically incorporate outputs from machine-learning-enhanced molecular dynamics to predict thermodynamic transition parameters.
Integrating atomistic simulation with CALPHAD overcomes limitations of solely empirical or purely atomistic methods.
The integrated approach can provide error margins within the combined inherent uncertainties of its constituent methods.
Predicted melting temperatures will be within approximately 5–10% of direct calorimetric measurements.
Fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting will be predicted with relative accuracy comparable to the stated 5–10% melting-temperature accuracy.
Predicted liquid-state thermodynamic properties will exhibit composition-correlated trends across different high-entropy-alloy systems.
Traditional experimental approaches require extensive testing for each alloy composition.
The framework is most applicable to high-entropy alloys having typical FCC or BCC motifs.
The framework may be less reliable for systems with strong magnetic ordering or phase segregation.
The framework may be less reliable when elemental interactions lie outside the machine-learning model's training set.
Model transferability to novel or extreme high-entropy-alloy compositions is uncertain.
The ability of CALPHAD coupling to capture all atomic-scale effects without additional empirical calibration is uncertain.

Consistent errors exceeding 10% for melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change across a significant subset of tested high-entropy alloys would falsify the proposed framework.
